terms.comment: The classical word for drunk, stretched to drugs, as Traupman and Morgan–Owens do; English “intoxicated” covers both in the same way.

evidence: Plin. NH 12.103: palma vescentēs inēbriat (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. intoxicate: inēbriārī, get high
terms.comment: inēbriō is to make drunk (Pliny, Seneca), so getting high is the passive, with the drug in the ablative of means.
The active inēbriāre means to make someone drunk, not to be drunk, and ā marks a person as agent, not a thing; say medicāmentīs psychotropicīs inēbriārī.

sources: Lewis & Short: ebrius · Lewis & Short: inebrio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 328.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. intoxicate; intoxicated, high.
